newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urged to require power plant divestments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urged to require power plant divestments.

text.p: The Federal government should mandate equity separation of power producers and distribution companies, Nancy Brockway told the first U.S. Department of Energy regional forum on electric industry restructuring.
The National Consumer Law Center representative said the federal government should, "leave the issues (of deregulation) to the states, but set floors, set standards".
She said one of the standards shoud be "complete equity separation between power suppliers and wire owners."

Richard Cowart, the chairman of Vermont's regulatory commission, told this first of four regional public meetings on deregulation that the federal role is to see that state efforts are not undercut by questions of authority.
It is "the obligation of the administration to create an environment where (deregulated) power sales and the environment" can both be achieved, he said.

Calling deregulation "an opportunity," he said it can be used to mandate use of renewable energy and "green labelling," which is requiring power suppliers to tell customers the source of their electricity and how much pollution it causes.

Responding to utility calls to recover investment that will be stranded, or become nonproductive, as the result of deregulation, Brockway said there will be "stranded cost recovery or rate relief. Take your choice."

Cheryl Harrington of the Regulatory Assistance Project said federal legislation must make it clear that the percentage of power coming from plants causing various forms of air pollution does not change.

Therefore, she pointed out, as nuclear power plants are decommissioned there will be an incentive to invest in renewable forms of energy that do not cause the pollution resulting from the burning of fossil fuels.
CINergy Corp general manager for environmental services, David Hoffman, pointed out "emissions go up (with deregulation) only if you assume no new (control) technology."

Stating, " I believe the environment is going to be the winner" with deregulation, Hoffman said the changes will give the U.S. a "unique opportunity to reinvent how we (utilities) do business in relationship to the environment."
